solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: One helps a writer issue a Mann novel

indicators.note: a novel thing is new and original, so the letters take on a fresh arrangement

blocks.note: taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: An assistant helps an author bring out a novel by Thomas Mann.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' reads as a noun, the book being issued, but it is the adjective telling you to rearrange. An AMANUENSIS is a literary assistant who takes dictation.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a secretary or scribe who takes dictation and copies manuscripts for an author.

clue.text: Biscuit pack trimmed in dark red

indicators.note: trimming cuts away the edges, so only the inner letters stay
one thing placed in another sits inside it

blocks.note: the word with its first and last letters cut off
maroon is a dark brownish red

explanation.surface: A packet of biscuits is cut open, revealing a deep red colour inside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pack' looks like the biscuit packet of the surface, but it just loses its ends; the insertion lands after the first letter of the colour.
explanation.definitionFit: A macaroon is a small sweet biscuit or cake made with ground almonds or coconut and egg white.

clue.text: Born in here, every second counts

indicators.note: only every second letter is counted, so alternate letters are kept

blocks.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of the two words run together

explanation.surface: A maternity ward where every second matters during a birth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Every second counts' sounds like urgency at a birth; it tells you to read only the even letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Née is the French-derived label placed before a woman's maiden name, literally meaning she was born with it.

clue.text: Raise spirits back from the dead

indicators.note: the back of a word is its final letter, so only that end is taken

blocks.note: the final letter of the word
the late means the recently dead

explanation.surface: A séance summons spirits back from the dead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raise spirits' and 'the dead' sound like a séance; 'spirits' is mood here, and 'back from' picks the last letter of 'the'.
explanation.definitionFit: To elate someone is to cheer them up and lift their mood, making them very happy.

clue.text: Mud, Fijian perhaps, lacks iodine

indicators.note: whatever something lacks is missing, so a letter is taken away

blocks.note: a Fijian is one example of someone from an island
I is the chemical symbol for iodine

explanation.surface: Pacific island mud turns out to contain no iodine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mud' looks like soil; it is mud in the sense of mudslinging. Removing the I from ISLANDER leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Mud here means damaging accusations, as in slinging mud, so it matches false spoken defamation of someone.

clue.text: Game one playing alone picked up

indicators.note: picking something up by ear means hearing it, so the sound matters rather than spelling

blocks.note: a soloist is a performer playing alone

explanation.surface: Someone playing a game on their own gets noticed.
explanation.walkthrough: Said aloud, the two-word card game runs together into the word for a lone performer.
explanation.definitionFit: Solo whist is a card game, a variant of whist where each player plays for themselves rather than in partnership.

clue.text: Pursue payment

blocks.note: first meaning: to carry on, as in carrying on a war or campaign
second meaning: money earned for work

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests chasing a debt; the two words are separate senses of one verb and noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a verb for carrying on a campaign or war, and a noun for the weekly pay a worker earns.

clue.text: “Oath”, perhaps, exactly as he said it

blocks.note: first meaning, read cryptically: 'oath' is a synonym for a solemn promise, as in giving your word
second meaning: quoted verbatim

explanation.surface: A witness repeats a sworn oath precisely as it was spoken.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half is whimsical: 'oath' is one term you could use in place of the noun meaning a promise, so it is literally a synonym for it.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means verbatim, reproducing someone's speech precisely in the same terms without change.

clue.text: Look up! Don’t stop and stare!

blocks.note: the opposite of stopping is going
to ogle is to stare lecherously

explanation.surface: Commands to someone: raise your eyes, keep moving, don't gawp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Look up!' reads as an order to raise your eyes; it is the definition, meaning to search for information.
explanation.definitionFit: To google something is to search for it online, the everyday way to consult a reference now.

clue.text: Plans a school wrestling team adopts

indicators.note: to adopt is to take someone into your family, so one piece is taken inside another
wrestlers twist and tangle, so the letters are twisted into a new order

blocks.note: SCH is a standard abbreviation for school
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A school's wrestling team takes on some new game plans.
explanation.walkthrough: The team takes in the A, and those five letters are rearranged after SCH.
explanation.definitionFit: Schemata is the Greek-style plural of schema, meaning outlines, diagrams or structured plans.

clue.text: Bacon piece Arnold reviewed

indicators.note: something re-viewed is looked at again in a different way, so its letters come out in another order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A critic called Arnold reviews a work by Francis Bacon.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the painter Francis Bacon and an art critic; 'Bacon piece' is actually meat.
explanation.definitionFit: A lardon is a small strip or cube of bacon or pork fat used in cooking.

clue.text: Fortune-teller’s line swallowed by old people

indicators.note: whatever is swallowed ends up inside the swallower

blocks.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old
a race is a people
L is an abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: An old tribe once swallowed a fortune-teller's prophecy wholesale.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is short for 'is', linking definition to wordplay; 'line' looks like a prophecy but is just a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An oracle was a priest or shrine through which the gods foretold the future, so a prophetic seer.

clue.text: Be focused and cordial

blocks.note: first meaning: to direct one's attention hard
second meaning: a fruit syrup diluted with water

explanation.surface: Advice to be attentive yet friendly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cordial' reads as the adjective meaning friendly; it is the noun, a sweet fruit drink sold undiluted. That drink is also called squash in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: A cordial is a sweet fruit syrup sold strong for diluting, and the verb means to fix one's attention.

clue.text: A contrarian’s comeuppance?

blocks.note: surface reading: the ruin that finally catches up with someone who always disagrees
setter's reading: a contrarian does the reverse of everything, so instead of coming up they would go down

explanation.walkthrough: Comeuppance is a deserved fall; turn 'come up' into its opposite, as a contrarian would, and you get a fall going the other way.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means ruin or collapse, a deserved loss of power or status, which fits a comeuppance.

clue.text: Threshold of a boom in air travel

definitions.text: Threshold of a boom in air travel

blocks.clueFragment: Threshold of a boom in air travel
blocks.note: surface reading: the point at which a surge in passenger flying takes off economically
setter's reading: a sonic boom is heard when an aircraft passes the speed of noise

explanation.walkthrough: A 'boom in air travel' sounds like an industry growth spurt; it is the bang of a supersonic jet, which occurs at this threshold.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the sharp rise in drag an aircraft meets approaching Mach 1, and crossing it produces a sonic boom.

clue.text: Giants hard to hide among six-footers

indicators.note: whatever hides among others is tucked away inside them

blocks.note: H is the pencil abbreviation for hard
bees and moths, both insects, which have six legs

explanation.surface: Giants find it difficult to conceal themselves among very tall people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Six-footers' suggests tall people; it means insects, whose six feet are legs. H slips in after BE.
explanation.definitionFit: A behemoth is a monstrous creature from the Bible, so anything enormous; the plural matches the noun giants.

clue.text: Soldier who runs waste tips in Exeter

indicators.note: the tips of a word are its two ends, so only those letters are kept

blocks.note: a desert is a waste, a barren expanse
the first and last letters of the city

explanation.surface: A soldier in Exeter is put in charge of rubbish dumps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Waste tips' reads as rubbish dumps and 'runs' as manages; the tips belong to Exeter, a city in Devon, and 'runs' means flees.
explanation.definitionFit: A deserter is a member of the armed forces who abandons their post without leave, fleeing duty.

clue.text: Award-winner artist briefly back on show

indicators.note: anything done briefly is cut short, so the word loses its final letter
going back means travelling the other way, so the letters are read in reverse

blocks.note: to exhibit is to show
Renoir is the French Impressionist painter

explanation.surface: A prize-winning artist returns briefly to the gallery for an exhibition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' in an across clue means placed after: the shortened, reversed painter follows EXHIBIT.
explanation.definitionFit: An exhibitioner is a student who holds an exhibition, a scholarship awarded by a school or college, especially at Oxford or Cambridge.

clue.text: Code of honour an ex-president papers over

blocks.note: either George Bush, a former US president
identity papers
O is the cricket scoring abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: A former president papers over a scandal despite his code of honour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Papers over' reads as covering up; the two words give separate pieces. In cricket an over is a set of six balls, abbreviated O.
explanation.definitionFit: Bushido is the samurai code of conduct in feudal Japan, stressing loyalty, courage and honourable behaviour.

clue.text: Expression of a former country’s disorder

indicators.note: an expression is something spoken, so the sound is what counts

blocks.note: the peninsula was once a single kingdom before its division into North and South

explanation.surface: A political slogan captures the chaos of a nation that no longer exists.
explanation.walkthrough: Korea as one state ended in 1945 with partition, hence 'former'. The 's stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Chorea is a nervous condition causing involuntary jerky movements, as in Huntington's or St Vitus' dance.

clue.text: Article by a newspaper

blocks.note: the definite article
as in multiplication: three by four means three times four

explanation.surface: A piece written for a newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' looks like a newspaper story; it is the grammar term. The Times is the sister of the Sunday Times, where this clue appeared.
explanation.definitionFit: The Times is a long-established London daily newspaper, founded in 1785, so one example of a newspaper.

clue.text: Club record set to be broken by United

indicators.note: something broken by another thing has that thing driven into it, splitting it

blocks.note: a compact disc is a record
jelly sets, or gels
U is the usual abbreviation for United in team names

explanation.surface: A football club's record is about to be broken by Manchester United.
explanation.walkthrough: The football surface hides a weapon: 'Club' is the definition, not a team, and 'set' is what jelly does.
explanation.definitionFit: A cudgel is a short thick stick used as a weapon, a club in the sense of a bludgeon.

clue.text: Sea life caught by the mouth

blocks.note: C is the cricket abbreviation for caught
oral means taken by mouth

explanation.surface: A fish is hooked through the mouth.
explanation.walkthrough: The fishing picture misleads: 'caught' is the scorecard abbreviation in cricket, and 'by the mouth' describes how medicine is taken.
explanation.definitionFit: Coral is made by colonies of tiny marine animals, polyps, forming reefs in warm oceans, so marine life.

clue.text: Gross painting that’s rushed inside

indicators.note: whatever is inside sits within something else

blocks.note: painting is art
ran means rushed

explanation.surface: An ugly picture that was hurriedly done indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gross' tempts you toward an adjective like crude for the painting; it means utter or flagrant.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean flagrant or out-and-out, as in arrant nonsense or gross negligence, describing something utter.

clue.text: Cook in boiling water

indicators.note: one thing placed in another sits within it

blocks.note: to cook the books is to rig them, falsify them
boiling with rage means furious

explanation.surface: A cooking instruction: boil it in water.
explanation.walkthrough: The kitchen picture is false: 'Cook' is to fiddle and 'boiling' is angry, and 'water' is a verb, the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To irrigate is to supply farmland with water through channels, so to water crops or fields.

clue.text: Break from knitting a pullover

indicators.note: taken from within the words, so the letters come straight out of them

blocks.note: the last letter of the first word, the second word, and the first letter of the third

explanation.surface: A knitter takes a rest from making a jumper.
explanation.walkthrough: A pullover is a jumper or sweater.
explanation.definitionFit: A gap is an interval or pause, a break in continuity or time.

clue.text: Prepared cheese rolls

indicators.note: something that rolls over turns round, so the word is read the other way

blocks.note: Edam is a Dutch cheese

explanation.surface: Bread rolls filled with cheese, ready to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rolls' looks like bread; it is the verb, turning the cheese round.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are past participles meaning got ready or put together, as a meal is made or prepared.

clue.text: Wet blanket left on babies

indicators.note: in an across answer, one thing on another comes after it, so this piece is placed second

blocks.note: to baby someone is to spoil them
port is the left side of a ship

explanation.surface: A damp blanket left lying on sleeping infants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Babies' is a verb, to pamper; 'on' in an across clue means the second piece follows the first.
explanation.definitionFit: A wet blanket is an idiom for someone who dampens others' fun, just as a killjoy does.
